nameStory: The bristly buttercup gets its name from two distinctive features: the cheerful yellow flowers that shine like freshly churned butter, and the stiff, bristly hairs that cover its stems and leaves. These tiny hairs give the plant a rough, almost sandpaper-like texture that makes it stand out from its smoother buttercup cousins. The scientific name 'hispidus' actually means 'bristly' or 'hairy' in Latin, so both the common and scientific names tell the same tactile story!
description: Bristly buttercup is a small, low-growing wildflower that rarely reaches more than a foot tall. Like other buttercups, it produces bright golden-yellow flowers with five glossy petals that seem to glow in the sunlight. What makes this species special is its notably hairy appearance - the entire plant is covered in stiff, bristly hairs that give it a rough texture. It's a perennial, meaning it comes back year after year from the same root system, forming small patches in suitable habitats.

idTips.label: Stems and Leaves
idTips.description: The entire plant feels distinctly bristly and rough to the touch, covered in stiff hairs that make it almost sandpaper-like compared to other buttercups. Run your fingers along the stem - you'll immediately notice the difference.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Classic buttercup flowers with five bright yellow, glossy petals that reflect light like tiny mirrors. The flowers are about half an inch across and have the typical buttercup's shiny, waxy appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A compact, low-growing plant that stays close to the ground, typically under one foot tall. It forms small clumps rather than spreading widely like some other buttercups.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The leaves are deeply divided into several lobes and covered with the same bristly hairs as the stems. They feel rough and coarse when touched, unlike the smoother leaves of most other buttercups.

habitat: Bristly buttercup prefers moist, partially shaded areas like woodland edges, stream banks, and meadow margins. It thrives in rich, somewhat damp soils and is often found in transitional zones between forests and open areas. Look for it in places that get some sunlight but aren't completely exposed, often growing alongside other spring wildflowers and native grasses.

seasonality.spring: This is prime time for bristly buttercup! The bright yellow flowers appear in late spring, usually May through early June, creating cheerful golden spots in woodland edges and moist meadows.
seasonality.summer: After flowering ends, the bristly foliage remains green and identifiable by its distinctive rough texture. Seeds develop and mature during this season.
seasonality.fall: The leaves may persist into early fall but become less prominent as they begin to yellow and die back. The plant's energy returns to its root system for winter.
seasonality.winter: The above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only the perennial root system underground waiting for spring's return.

funFact: The bristly hairs on this buttercup aren't just for show - they're actually a defensive strategy! These tiny spines make the plant much less appealing to hungry herbivores like deer and rabbits, giving it a survival advantage over its smoother, more edible buttercup relatives.
confusionNotes: With only 5 recorded sightings in New England, bristly buttercup is easily confused with the much more common meadow buttercup and other yellow buttercups. The key is in the touch test - if the stems and leaves feel distinctly rough and bristly like coarse sandpaper, you've likely found the bristly buttercup. Other buttercups feel much smoother to the touch.
contextualKnowledge: Like all buttercups, this plant contains compounds that make it toxic if eaten, so it's strictly a 'look but don't taste' wildflower. The extremely low observation count in New England (only 5 recorded sightings) suggests this species may be quite rare in our region or easily overlooked due to its similarity to other buttercups.
compareHints: Among New England's many buttercups, bristly buttercup stands out primarily for its rough, hairy texture - most other species like meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup have relatively smooth stems and leaves. While early buttercup is also somewhat hairy, it's typically smaller and blooms much earlier in the season. The combination of late spring blooming, bright yellow flowers, and distinctly bristly texture makes this species unique in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buttercups, small-flowered buttercup is unmistakable due to its tiny petals - all other buttercup species have much more prominent yellow flowers.
Among New England's buttercups, hooked buttercup is unique for its woodland habitat and tiny, pale flowers—most other buttercups prefer sunny, open areas and have much brighter, larger yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercup species, meadow buttercup stands out for its tall, upright growth and deeply palm-divided leaves.
Unlike meadow buttercup which grows in upright clumps, or bulbous buttercup with its swollen stem base, creeping buttercup is the only common buttercup that spreads by runners along the ground.
Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base.
Unlike other New England buttercups that have bright, showy yellow flowers, cursed crowfoot has tiny, pale, almost insignificant blooms.
Among New England buttercups, bristly crowfoot stands out for its rough, hairy texture and pale flowers - most other buttercups have smoother leaves and bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercups, yellow water-crowfoot is one of the few truly aquatic species, distinguished by its floating stems and dramatic leaf differences between air and water.
Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves.
Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup with their typical three-lobed leaves, fen crowfoot has leaves so finely divided they look almost thread-like.

Among New England's many buttercups, early buttercup stands out for its combination of very early bloom time, preference for dry rather than moist habitats, and distinctively narrow, deeply-cut leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which grows tall and robust in fields, Allegheny Mountain buttercup stays much smaller and more delicate.
Rock buttercup stands out from other New England buttercups by having the smallest, palest flowers in the family - most other buttercups have bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among the 20+ buttercup species in New England, lesser spearwort stands out immediately because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves – all other buttercups have lobed, divided, or rounded leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which prefers drier ground and grows much taller, swamp buttercup stays low and spreads along wet soil.
Among New England's aquatic buttercups, longbeak buttercup is distinguished by its exceptionally long fruit beaks and preference for flowing water.

Unlike terrestrial buttercups like meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup, small yellow water-crowfoot is adapted for aquatic life with thicker, more succulent leaves and a strictly prostrate growth habit.
Unlike all other New England buttercups that grow upright, Lapland buttercup stays completely flat and creeping.
Among New England's many buttercups, water-plantain spearwort is unique for its completely undivided, lance-shaped leaves - most other buttercups have deeply lobed or divided leaves.
Unlike its terrestrial buttercup cousins that have typical yellow flowers, thread-leaved water-crowfoot has white petals with yellow centers and specialized underwater foliage.
